neighborhood_overview:
Poble Sec is a very attractive area that combines the peacefulness of Montjuïc's large green spaces with the proximity of Barcelona's lively centre in less than 15 minutes between the two.

Poble Sec is a laid back district, full of shops, supermarkets, restaurants, bars and cafés with terraces. You might be overwhelmed with the amount of options you have when it comes to grabbing a bite to eat. The Plaça del Sortidor and the pedestrianized Carrer de Blai are two of the most popular zones amongst locals to go to eat. The world famous bar "Quimet i Quimet" is just a one minute walk from the apartment.

Traffic speed is limited to 30km/h (19miles/h) in all the area.

neighborhood_overview:
Enjoy the authentic & trendy neighborhood of Gracia. One of the hippest, most cosmopolitan areas in the city, Gracia is both culturally and artistically distinct from the rest of Barcelona. Its eclectic charm attracts travelers from all over though the majority of its inhabitants are local. Gracia’s old, one-way streets are organized around a series of plazas, including Plaça de Vila de Gracia, Plaça del Sol and Plaça de la Virreina among many others where people of all ages gather everyday and night. All, just a few blocks from the apartment.

During the day, the “hipster” barrio is full of life, projecting a hip and edgy vibe. At night the environment transforms, and although the narrow streets are quiet and peaceful, nightlife in Gracia is vibrant. The neighborhood is full of small cafes serving classic Spanish tapas and Catalonian specialties as well as a surprising array of restaurants offering ethnic cuisines ranging from Japanese to Greek.

description:
Exclusive 135m² (1,450 sq. ft.) penthouse with a stunning terrace in Gràcia, a trendy neighborhood in the heart of Barcelona. Renovated in 2022, it is located next to Fontana metro station and surrounded by local markets, shops, and restaurants. Major landmarks are within walking distance.

neighborhood_overview:
Gràcia is a one of the most authentic neighborhoods in Barcelona. It is located in the center of Barcelona, but there is a small town feeling wherever you walk, especially in the squares, where the locals spend their free time.

Here you will find a mixture of bohemian, trendy and traditional. This is mirrored in the new design boutiques that thrive everywhere. The gastronomical offer is quite diverse, ranging from take away pizza and sushi restaurants, to high quality catalan food.

Verdi is one of its most iconic streets. Here you can start off with drinks and tapas, then attend a movie theatre and watch a film in original version, have Egyptian food for dinner and enjoy Italian ice cream for dessert.

The neighborhood is famous in Barcelona thanks to its local holiday. La Festa Major de Gràcia is one of the biggest local festivities, held every August. During this week long festival, the residents decorate their streets with very creative motifs.

name: Sonder Vasanta | King Room
description: Welcome to Vasanta, your ticket to an iconic Barcelona experience. The cheerful yellow exterior sits on an octagonal block within the Eixample neighborhood. Each space inside features high ceilings and plenty of natural light. Outside, the city is ripe for exploration. You're a short walk away from tree-lined shopping through Rambla de Catalunya. neighborhood_overview: As Barcelona’s most recognizable neighborhood, Eixample is a late 19th-century urban development known for its dazzling Art Nouveau architecture. Named the "Expansion" in Catalan, the district is characterized by its geometric grid layout and is located north of Plaça de Catalunya. Admire Modernist townhouses that line the main streets, or stop by a cozy sidewalk café to people-watch while sipping a café con leche or cortado. Don’t miss the chance to visit Casa Batlló, Casa Milà, and the unfinished Sagrada Familia, all stunning attractions designed by world-famous Catalan architect, Antoni Gaudí. The spectacular gothic Cathedral of Barcelona overlooks thriving boutiques and cafés along stone-paved streets that are ripe for exploration and afternoon ambling.  Meandering alleyways and arched passages open to tranquil sunlit plaças and to the teeming avenues of La Rambla and Via Leitana which flank the neighborhood. Intricate wrought-iron street lamps illuminate the quarter as it transforms into its evening splendor. Bars and restaurants burst into activity on flourishing squares like Plaça Reial, while the nightlife crowd spills in and out of the secluded spots of narrower streets.

neighborhood_overview: The Eixample is the Catalan Art Nouveau center of the city. The area was built in the late 19th and early 20th century and the architecture of the neighbourhood is stunning, with some real gems to explore. A few steps from your apartment you’ll be able to feast your eyes on amazing buildings such as Gaudí’s Casa Batlló and the lesser-known but stunning Casa Amatller. The area is one of the cultural and shopping hearts of the city. You’ll find designer stores and high street brands next to all sorts of great restaurants and bars. A short walk (15 minutes) will get you to the bustling old city, where you’ll have another great selection of shops, markets, museums, art galleries, restaurants and bars to choose from. The area boasts great transport links and you’ll be able to get to all ends of the city in a few minutes by subway, bus or taxi.

neighborhood_overview:
The charming gothic quarter is one of the most symbolic areas of Barcelona with its meandering narrow streets that are an invitation to discover all kinds of hidden gems like small bars, restaurants, and boutiques.

The Barcelona Gothic Quarter, or Barri Gòtic, is the historic heart of the city, characterized by narrow medieval streets, Gothic architecture, and vibrant street life. Centered around the Barcelona Cathedral, it features ancient Roman walls, Gothic churches, charming plazas, and museums. Construction: Plaza España was designed for the 1929 International Exposition, and its design was handled by architects Josep Puig i Cadafalch and Guillem Busquets, though it was completed by Pere Domènech i Roura.
Importance: It is one of the main hubs of the city, connecting the city center with Montjuïc, one of Barcelona's most important cultural and recreational areas.

Notable Features
Plaza España Fountain:

Designed by Josep Maria Jujol (a collaborator of Antoni Gaudí).
It represents allegories of Spain's rivers and seas, with sculptures inspired by classical mythology.
Venetian Towers:

Inspired by the Campanile of Venice.
They act as a monumental gateway leading to Montjuïc.

neighborhood_overview:
The Eixample district not only is the most iconic in Barcelona, it’s also the most diverse in terms of shopping, restaurants and nightlife. The gridlike layout is the symbol of the sunny and modern Barcelona we know today.

Eixample, which translates as ""extension"" in recognition of its status as the newer part of the city, is a large area north of Plaça de Catalunya spreading left and right of Passeig de Gràcia. The area is indeed an extension to the city that benefits greatly from its ingenious urban planning at the hands of Catalan engineer Ildefons Cerdà in the 1850s. Cerdà had a fondness for straight lines. Therefore, the whole area is set out in a grid with each block having an inner courtyard. This means that it is hard to get lost in Eixample, and moreover, easy to find places.

neighborhood_overview:
Welcome to Casa Wilson, nestled in the vibrant Gràcia neighborhood just a stones throw from Plaça Rovira i Trias, a charming hub that captures both the history and energy of Barcelona. Named after Antoni Rovira i Trias, a celebrated local architect and urban planner, the square honors him with a life-sized bronze sculpture seated on a bench, overlooking the area he helped design. Known also as Plaça dels Tres Senyors, this square reflects old Gràcia, when it was a village surrounded by rural lands owned by three prominent families.
Beyond the square, Gràcia’s bohemian spirit and artistic flair come to life. Winding streets are filled with boutique shops, cozy cafés, and bustling markets where locals and visitors alike enjoy the lively yet relaxed pace of life. With vibrant plazas where musicians, artists, and neighbors gather, Gràcia feels like a small town within the city—a place that’s warm, welcoming, and full of charm.

Elegant Villa de Gràcia has incredible cultural attractions, hip boutiques and artist studios, and a wonderful nightlife scene. In addition to the Plaça del Sol's outdoor cafes, residents can enjoy live performances at the Teatrenu theater or see a movie at the Verdi Barcelona theater.

neighborhood_overview:
Modern Barcelona was born in L’Eixample, devised by the engineer and urban planner to whom he owes his magical and unique drawing: Ildefons Cerdà. With its urban plan, Cerdà designed an egalitarian city, where neighborhoods are not differentiated from others and public services are distributed evenly throughout every corner.

The district is the result of one of the most splendid moments in the city's history, when it is definitely configured as the engine of contemporary Catalonia and breaks with the medieval past knocking down the walls. L’Eixample was built in the years of the industrialization of Catalonia, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The central part, the Dreta de l'Eixample, was the bourgeoisie neighborhood that introduced into its home a style of its own, modernism.

L’Eixample is formed by six neighborhoods: La Dreta de l’Eixample, Old Esquerra de l’Eixample, Nova Esquerra de l’Eixample, Fort Pienc, Sagrada Família and Sant Antoni.

neighborhood_overview:
The apartment is conveniently located 5 minutes away Paseo de Gracia avenue and in the very middle of Eisample district. This elegant, majestic boulevard was a showcase for Barcelona's bourgeoisie at the turn of the 19th century, and links the Plaça Catalunya with the district of Gràcia, hence its name. The presence of Barcelona's finest modernista buildings makes this avenue a veritable open-air museum.

Barcelona's new artery, in the centre of the newly built Eixample district, was the place moneyed bourgeois families chose to live. On either side of the street, they constructed imposing buildings that continue to delight everyone who passes by. These jewels of Catalonia's home-grown art nouveau, modernisme, and the later movement, noucentisme, were created by architects of the calibre of Gaudí (La Pedrera and the Casa Batlló), Puig i Cadafalch (casa Amatller), and Domènech i Muntaner (Casa Lleó Morera), to name just three.
